issues.item: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: This trigger is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For a 21-year-old married male relief worker in a war zone, military topics and Arabic shouting fit the reported trauma context, but 'my ex' is relationship-specific and not plausibly linked to the war-zone trauma as presented. It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette:
Lukas Weber was 21, newly married, and working as a social ministry worker when he was deployed with a relief team to a war zone. Before he left, he had imagined long days of distributing supplies, helping families find shelter, and doing work that felt morally clear. What stayed with him instead was one specific incident that seemed to split his life into a before and after. His team had been moving through a crowded area during a period of heightened tension, trying to coordinate aid delivery among frightened civilians. The scene was loud and compressed, with people pushing close, voices rising, and men shouting in Arabic from different directions. Lukas did not understand the words, only the force in them, and he remembered the sound as urgent and jagged, the kind of shouting that made everyone around him move at once. In that moment, strangers were suddenly too near, bodies turned sharply, arms lifted, and the crowd's movements became impossible for him to read. He had felt overtaken by terror, certain that something catastrophic was happening around him even before he could make sense of it.

When he spoke about that day now, he often faltered because the memory did not feel organized like an ordinary story. He would say that it was so extreme it was hard to believe it had actually happened to him. At times he described it almost as if he were recounting something he had watched happen to somebody else, and then, without warning, the distance would collapse. If he tried to talk through the event in detail, the same terror came back into his body so fast that he lost the sense that it was over. He did not experience it as a past event he was remembering; he experienced it as if he were there again, caught in noise, movement, and danger. Even in session, when he began to approach the most vivid parts, his posture changed, his eyes tracked the room, and he seemed to brace for something immediate.

After returning home to the United States, Lukas found that seemingly ordinary moments could throw him back into that state. At work in social ministry, military topics came up often enough to unsettle him. A visiting speaker mentioning troop movements, a parishioner discussing a family member's deployment, or even a casual conversation about war on the edge of a community meeting could make his attention narrow and his body tense. The most potent moments were auditory. If he heard shouting in Arabic in a video clip, on someone's phone, or from a passing group in the city, he reacted before he could think, his body going rigid and alert. What frightened him most was how quickly sudden movements by other people affected him. If a stranger stepped toward him unexpectedly in a hallway or turned abruptly during food distribution, he was immediately on guard, as if ordinary approach might conceal danger. He had come to feel threatened by strangers in everyday situations, even when part of him knew he was standing in a church office or on a sidewalk at home.

Nights became difficult in a different way. Lukas delayed sleep by staying up very late, sometimes sitting with the television on or scrolling pointlessly on his phone until exhaustion forced him to lie down. He told himself he was not tired, but he also knew that going to sleep meant becoming vulnerable to waking in panic. When he did sleep, he often woke during the night and checked whether he was safe, scanning the apartment, listening for sounds, making sure doors were secure. His wife noticed that he startled easily and seemed to be listening for something even in silence.

Over the following months, Lukas's inner life narrowed. He spent long stretches ruminating about how the event could have been prevented, replaying choices, timing, and decisions, as if there might still be a way to revise what had happened if he thought hard enough. At the same time, he began avoiding situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful. Invitations from his wife to celebrate small things, spend time with friends, or plan for the future were met with hesitation or withdrawal. Bright, enjoyable moments felt wrong to him, almost unsafe, and he kept himself at a distance from them. The cost of that was becoming visible in his marriage; his wife experienced him as physically present but emotionally difficult to reach, especially when she tried to reconnect him with ordinary young-married life.

By the time Lukas sought help, it was not because the event had become easier to understand, but because his world had become so organized around bracing, checking, and holding himself apart. What finally pushed him to come in was the realization that even in the ministry setting he cared about, he was orienting less to the people in front of him than to possible threat around them. He said he was afraid that if he talked about what happened, he would be pulled fully back into it, and afraid too that he was becoming someone his wife no longer recognized. At the same time, he still hoped that help might allow him to sleep without guarding the night and to hear the past spoken of as past, rather than feeling it arrive all over again.
